## Countries That Banned All Corporal Punishment Between 1955-2004

According to the data from End Corporal Punishment (Every Child Protected), the following countries banned **all forms** of corporal punishment of children (including in homes, schools, and institutions) between 1955 and 2004:

| Year | Country |
|------|---------|
| 1979 | Sweden |
| 1983 | Finland |
| 1987 | Norway |
| 1989 | Austria |
| 1994 | Cyprus |
| 1997 | Denmark |
| 1998 | Latvia |
| 1999 | Croatia |
| 2000 | Germany, Israel, Bulgaria |
| 2002 | Turkmenistan |
| 2003 | Iceland |
| 2004 | Romania, Ukraine |

## Under-5 Mortality Rate Analysis (2005-2023)

I analyzed the World Bank Group under-5 mortality rate data for these countries. Looking for declines of **more than 3 per 1,000 live births** between 2005 and 2023:

### Qualifying Countries (Decline > 3/1,000):

1. **Romania**: Decline of approximately **43 per 1,000** (from ~79/1,000 in 2004-2005 to ~36/1,000 in 2023)

2. **Ukraine**: Decline of approximately **40 per 1,000** (from ~80/1,000 in 2004-2005 to ~40/1,000 in 2023)

### Other Countries with Notable But Lower Declines:

- **Ethiopia** (not in the ban list): ~12.5/1,000 decline
- **Madagascar** (not in the ban list): ~12.3/1,000 decline  
- **Lesotho** (not in the ban list): ~3.1/1,000 decline
- **Ghana** (not in the ban list): ~2.0/1,000 decline
- **India** (not in the ban list): ~5.5/1,000 decline
- **Kenya** (not in the ban list): ~6.3/1,000 decline
- **Malaysia** (not in the ban list): ~0.7/1,000 decline

## Answer

Among the countries that banned all corporal punishment of children between 1955 and 2004, **two countries** had under-5 mortality rates that decreased by more than 3 per 1,000 live births between 2005 and 2023 according to World Bank Group data:

1. **Romania** (banned in 2004)
2. **Ukraine** (banned in 2004)

Both countries show dramatic mortality reductions, with Romania declining approximately 43 deaths per 1,000 and Ukraine declining approximately 40 deaths per 1,000 over this period.

In upholding section 43, the majority of the Court provided considerable guidance to the interpretation of the provision. The majority held that the person administering the discipline must be a parent or legal guardian, or in some cases, a school teacher (i.e. non-parental relatives such as grandparents, aunts, or uncles, as well as babysitters and other caretakers, are banned from spanking); that the force must be used "by way of correction" (sober, reasoned uses of force that address the actual behaviour of the child and are designed to restrain, control or express some symbolic disapproval of his or her behaviour), that the child must be capable of benefiting from the correction (i.e. not under the age of 2 or over 12), and that the use of force must be "reasonable under the circumstances", meaning that it results neither in harm nor in the prospect of bodily harm. Punishment involving slaps or blows to the head is harmful, the Court held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-33) Use of any implement other than a bare hand is illegal and hitting a child in anger or in retaliation for something a child did is not considered reasonable and is against the law. The Court defined "reasonable" as force that would have a "transitory and trifling" impact on the child. For example, spanking or slapping a child so hard that it leaves a mark that lasts for several hours would not be considered "transitory and trifling".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-34)
Among the recommendations of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, formed to redress the legacy of the Canadian Indian residential school system, is a call to repeal Section 43 of the Criminal Code.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-35)
On 23 March 2021, the Senate of Colombia unanimously voted to approve a bill that prohibits physical punishment, cruel, humiliating, or degrading acts, and violence as forms of correctional approaches for the upbringing of children and adolescents in Colombia.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-36)

Until 2026, the Czech Republic had remained the only country in the European Union that does not outlaw child corporal punishment or plan to introduce such a law.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-37) On July 17, 2025, the president signed an amendment to the Civil Code, making corporal punishment of children explicitly prohibited by law, beginning January 1, 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-cz-16)
Corporal punishment in schools in Denmark became explicitly prohibited in 1967 and in 1985, parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children became outlawed through a new law which required parents "to protect their child from physical and psychological violence and other humiliating treatment".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-39) However, the law was believed to still support corporal punishment as there was a controversy whether the law permitted parents to punish their children physically or otherwise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-40) Therefore, after several years of debate, a new, clearer law came into force on 28 May 1997, providing that "_The child has right to care and security. It must be treated with respect for its person and must not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment_".
Denmark's autonomous territories, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, banned corporal punishment of children in 2007 and 2016, respectively.

School corporal punishment was banned in 1914.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-41) Parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was outlawed in 1969 when the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, stating that a "petty assault" was not punishable if committed by parents or others who exercise their right to chastise a child, was removed. In 1983, corporal punishment of children was explicitly banned.
In the Napoleonic era parents were explicitly allowed to physically punish their children. Spanking was previously popular, with 85% of French parents admitting to using it. However, in 2019, the National Assembly approved a bill introducing a complete ban on all forms of physical punishment of children and required mayors officiating at civil weddings to remind couples that violence against children is unlawful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-auto-7) The law makes corporal punishment a civil offense, not a criminal one.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-42)
School corporal punishment was prohibited in East Germany (which became part of the Federal Republic of Germany at the German reunification on 3 October 1990). In the Federal Republic (West Germany before reunification), it was prohibited at different times in its different states between 1975 and 1983.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-43)

In the Federal Republic of Germany, in 1980 it became prohibited for parents to educate their children with "degrading measures" (it was not clear exactly what "degrading" meant), of which the common interpretation was that corporal punishment of children was still permitted as long as it was not "degrading". On 1 July 1998, corporal punishment was outlawed through a new law stating that "Degrading educational measures, especially physical and psychological maltreatment, are inadmissible"; the common interpretation of that law was that parents still had some right to use corporal punishment on their children. In November 2000, that law was replaced with a new more clear and strict law stating that "_Children have right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological violence and other degrading educational measures are inadmissible._"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-45)
The 2006 enacted Law 3500/06 on the treatment of domestic violence prohibits the use of physical violence against a minor as a means of punishment in the context of his upbringing, with the explicit clarification - in the explanatory memorandum - that corporal punishment is not included. to the permissible penitentiary measures of article 1518 of the Civil Code and that its use entails for the parents the consequences of the bad exercise of parental care.
Specifically, Article 4 provides that physical violence against minors as a means of punishment in the context of their upbringing brings about the consequences of Article 1532 of the Civil Code. The explanatory memorandum to this article states, among other things: “The regulation of Article 4 makes it clear that corporal punishment against children is not included in the permissible punishment measures of Article 1518 of the Civil Code in accordance with modern pedagogical views. It constitutes a case of poor exercise of custody and for this reason brings about the application of article 1532 of the Civil Code. According to this article, in such a case, the court may order any appropriate measure. "Any act of inflicting pain or physical discomfort on a minor should be treated as physical violence, with the aim of punishing or controlling his behavior."

In Ireland, all forms of corporal punishment of children have been definitively outlawed since the passing of the Children First Act 2015.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46)Law in the Republic of Ireland inherited the pre-independence common law and statutes modelled on English law. These included allowance under common law of "physical chastisement" by teachers, and under the Children Act 1908 (8 Edw. 7. c. 67) of "reasonable chastisement" by parents and those _in loco parentis_.

In June 2021, the Spanish Parliament passed a new, pioneering child and adolescent protection law against all kinds of violence or abuse. It was championed by the British-Spanish pianist James Rhodes and the left-wing party Unidas Podemos, but eventually supported by all political groups in Parliament except Vox. A Code of Minors is also being drafted.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain3-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain4-83)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain0-80)
Sweden was the world's first nation to outlaw all corporal punishment of children in 1966, when the law that permitted parents to use corporal punishment of their children became removed and fully replaced with the constitution of assault under the Penal Code; however, even though the law no longer supported parents' right to use physical punishment of their children, it was believed to still be permitted (as there was no explicit ban). School corporal punishment was already banned since 1958.
On 1 July 1979, Sweden became the world's first nation to explicitly ban corporal punishment of children, through an amendment to the Parenthood and Guardianship Code which stated, "Children are entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. Children are to be treated with respect for their person and individuality and may not be subjected to corporal punishment or any other humiliating treatment." In Parliament - the law was supported 259 to 6 with 3 abstentions.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Modig-85) Corporal punishment in Sweden is not seen as a separate legal issue - but is handled according to the criteria for assault.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)

One thing that helped pave the way for the ban was a 1971 murder case where a 3-year-old girl was beaten to death by her stepfather. The case shook the general public and preventing child abuse became a political hot topic for years to come.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-87)
It is estimated that approximately 5% of Swedish children continue to be illegally spanked, however, in addition to being unlawful, physical punishment of children is now considered socially unacceptable.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-88)
On September 26, 2025, both chambers of the Federal Assembly approved the inclusion of "non-violent parenting" in Swiss law. The law forbids "physical punishment and other forms of degrading treatment". The Federal Council is to decide at the beginning of 2026 when the new law start to take effect.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-ch-17)
In Turkey, corporal punishment is unlawful, considered assault,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-89) and is punishable by imprisonment for a term not less than 1 year and not more than 3 years if none of the special cases below occur.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-90)
If the courts deem that any one of:

*   "the victim is physically or psychologically unable to defend themselves",  
*   the victim is the child of the perpetrator, or  
*   a weapon (which is defined to include "anything used in defense or offense"[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-91)) is used in the act is true, the punishment is increased by half of the original amount.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-92) If the courts deem that the perpetrator acted in a "fiendish" way, the punishment is increased to twice the original amount.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-93) If either one or both of these are true, it is said that the act was "egregious".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-94)
If the victim suffers, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:
*   persistent weakness in any of their senses or organs,  
*   persistent hardship in speaking,  
*   a permanent mark on their face, or  
*   a danger to their life,
the punishment determined above is increased to twice its final amount (determined above).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-95) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 3 years, or 5 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-96)
Alternatively, if the victim, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:
*   begins to suffer from an illness for which there is no cure, or, enters a persistent vegetative state,  
*   suffers a complete loss of function to one of their senses or organs,  
*   loses the ability to speak or to reproduce, or  
*   a permanent change to their face,

the punishment determined above is increased to thrice its final amount (determined above).[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-97) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 5 years, or 8 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-98)
If the victim suffers a broken bone as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, the courts may increase the final punishment by up to half its original amount, depending on the vitality of the broken bone to daily life.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-99)
If the victim dies as a result of corporal punishment being used on them but the act does not meet the criteria for murder, the final punishment must be imprisonment for a term not less than 8 years and not more than 12 years. If the act was found to be "egregious", the term of imprisonment must be between 12 and 18 years.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-100)
In the United Kingdom, the law regarding domestic corporal punishment varies by jurisdiction.

Where in the world is smacking children illegal?
70 countries have taken the step of prohibiting all corporal punishment of children, including within the family home.
Sweden led the way in 1979. Since then, countries across the world have recognised that children deserve protection from physical punishment.
Yet in England, Northern Ireland, the USA, Canada and Australia, physical punishment by parents remains lawful in certain circumstances.
There is a difference between what is legally permitted and what we know about child development.
Children need boundaries, guidance and consequences. They do not need to experience physical pain to learn.
If we would not accept an adult being hit to teach them a lesson, why should we accept it for a child?
Protecting children from physical punishment is not about removing discipline. It is about recognising their right to safety, dignity and respect.

In upholding section 43, the majority of the Court provided considerable guidance to the interpretation of the provision. The majority held that the person administering the discipline must be a parent or legal guardian, or in some cases, a school teacher (i.e. non-parental relatives such as grandparents, aunts, or uncles, as well as babysitters and other caretakers, are banned from spanking); that the force must be used "by way of correction" (sober, reasoned uses of force that address the actual behaviour of the child and are designed to restrain, control or express some symbolic disapproval of his or her behaviour), that the child must be capable of benefiting from the correction (i.e. not under the age of 2 or over 12), and that the use of force must be "reasonable under the circumstances", meaning that it results neither in harm nor in the prospect of bodily harm. Punishment involving slaps or blows to the head is harmful, the Court held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-33) Use of any implement other than a bare hand is illegal and hitting a child in anger or in retaliation for something a child did is not considered reasonable and is against the law. The Court defined "reasonable" as force that would have a "transitory and trifling" impact on the child. For example, spanking or slapping a child so hard that it leaves a mark that lasts for several hours would not be considered "transitory and trifling".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-34)
Among the recommendations of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, formed to redress the legacy of the Canadian Indian residential school system, is a call to repeal Section 43 of the Criminal Code.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-35)
On 23 March 2021, the Senate of Colombia unanimously voted to approve a bill that prohibits physical punishment, cruel, humiliating, or degrading acts, and violence as forms of correctional approaches for the upbringing of children and adolescents in Colombia.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-36)

Until 2026, the Czech Republic had remained the only country in the European Union that does not outlaw child corporal punishment or plan to introduce such a law.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-37) On July 17, 2025, the president signed an amendment to the Civil Code, making corporal punishment of children explicitly prohibited by law, beginning January 1, 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-cz-16)
Corporal punishment in schools in Denmark became explicitly prohibited in 1967 and in 1985, parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children became outlawed through a new law which required parents "to protect their child from physical and psychological violence and other humiliating treatment".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-39) However, the law was believed to still support corporal punishment as there was a controversy whether the law permitted parents to punish their children physically or otherwise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-40) Therefore, after several years of debate, a new, clearer law came into force on 28 May 1997, providing that "_The child has right to care and security. It must be treated with respect for its person and must not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment_".
Denmark's autonomous territories, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, banned corporal punishment of children in 2007 and 2016, respectively.
texts.6:
School corporal punishment was banned in 1914.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-41) Parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was outlawed in 1969 when the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, stating that a "petty assault" was not punishable if committed by parents or others who exercise their right to chastise a child, was removed. In 1983, corporal punishment of children was explicitly banned.
In the Napoleonic era parents were explicitly allowed to physically punish their children. Spanking was previously popular, with 85% of French parents admitting to using it. However, in 2019, the National Assembly approved a bill introducing a complete ban on all forms of physical punishment of children and required mayors officiating at civil weddings to remind couples that violence against children is unlawful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-auto-7) The law makes corporal punishment a civil offense, not a criminal one.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-42)
School corporal punishment was prohibited in East Germany (which became part of the Federal Republic of Germany at the German reunification on 3 October 1990). In the Federal Republic (West Germany before reunification), it was prohibited at different times in its different states between 1975 and 1983.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-43)
texts.7:
In the Federal Republic of Germany, in 1980 it became prohibited for parents to educate their children with "degrading measures" (it was not clear exactly what "degrading" meant), of which the common interpretation was that corporal punishment of children was still permitted as long as it was not "degrading". On 1 July 1998, corporal punishment was outlawed through a new law stating that "Degrading educational measures, especially physical and psychological maltreatment, are inadmissible"; the common interpretation of that law was that parents still had some right to use corporal punishment on their children. In November 2000, that law was replaced with a new more clear and strict law stating that "_Children have right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological violence and other degrading educational measures are inadmissible._"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-45)
The 2006 enacted Law 3500/06 on the treatment of domestic violence prohibits the use of physical violence against a minor as a means of punishment in the context of his upbringing, with the explicit clarification - in the explanatory memorandum - that corporal punishment is not included. to the permissible penitentiary measures of article 1518 of the Civil Code and that its use entails for the parents the consequences of the bad exercise of parental care.
Specifically, Article 4 provides that physical violence against minors as a means of punishment in the context of their upbringing brings about the consequences of Article 1532 of the Civil Code. The explanatory memorandum to this article states, among other things: “The regulation of Article 4 makes it clear that corporal punishment against children is not included in the permissible punishment measures of Article 1518 of the Civil Code in accordance with modern pedagogical views. It constitutes a case of poor exercise of custody and for this reason brings about the application of article 1532 of the Civil Code. According to this article, in such a case, the court may order any appropriate measure. "Any act of inflicting pain or physical discomfort on a minor should be treated as physical violence, with the aim of punishing or controlling his behavior."
texts.8: In Ireland, all forms of corporal punishment of children have been definitively outlawed since the passing of the Children First Act 2015.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46)Law in the Republic of Ireland inherited the pre-independence common law and statutes modelled on English law. These included allowance under common law of "physical chastisement" by teachers, and under the Children Act 1908 (8 Edw. 7. c. 67) of "reasonable chastisement" by parents and those _in loco parentis_.

In June 2021, the Spanish Parliament passed a new, pioneering child and adolescent protection law against all kinds of violence or abuse. It was championed by the British-Spanish pianist James Rhodes and the left-wing party Unidas Podemos, but eventually supported by all political groups in Parliament except Vox. A Code of Minors is also being drafted.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain3-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain4-83)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain0-80)
Sweden was the world's first nation to outlaw all corporal punishment of children in 1966, when the law that permitted parents to use corporal punishment of their children became removed and fully replaced with the constitution of assault under the Penal Code; however, even though the law no longer supported parents' right to use physical punishment of their children, it was believed to still be permitted (as there was no explicit ban). School corporal punishment was already banned since 1958.
On 1 July 1979, Sweden became the world's first nation to explicitly ban corporal punishment of children, through an amendment to the Parenthood and Guardianship Code which stated, "Children are entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. Children are to be treated with respect for their person and individuality and may not be subjected to corporal punishment or any other humiliating treatment." In Parliament - the law was supported 259 to 6 with 3 abstentions.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Modig-85) Corporal punishment in Sweden is not seen as a separate legal issue - but is handled according to the criteria for assault.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)

One thing that helped pave the way for the ban was a 1971 murder case where a 3-year-old girl was beaten to death by her stepfather. The case shook the general public and preventing child abuse became a political hot topic for years to come.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-87)
It is estimated that approximately 5% of Swedish children continue to be illegally spanked, however, in addition to being unlawful, physical punishment of children is now considered socially unacceptable.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-88)
On September 26, 2025, both chambers of the Federal Assembly approved the inclusion of "non-violent parenting" in Swiss law. The law forbids "physical punishment and other forms of degrading treatment". The Federal Council is to decide at the beginning of 2026 when the new law start to take effect.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-ch-17)
In Turkey, corporal punishment is unlawful, considered assault,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-89) and is punishable by imprisonment for a term not less than 1 year and not more than 3 years if none of the special cases below occur.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-90)
If the courts deem that any one of:
texts.17:
*   "the victim is physically or psychologically unable to defend themselves",  
*   the victim is the child of the perpetrator, or  
*   a weapon (which is defined to include "anything used in defense or offense"[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-91)) is used in the act is true, the punishment is increased by half of the original amount.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-92) If the courts deem that the perpetrator acted in a "fiendish" way, the punishment is increased to twice the original amount.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-93) If either one or both of these are true, it is said that the act was "egregious".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-94)
If the victim suffers, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:
*   persistent weakness in any of their senses or organs,  
*   persistent hardship in speaking,  
*   a permanent mark on their face, or  
*   a danger to their life,
the punishment determined above is increased to twice its final amount (determined above).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-95) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 3 years, or 5 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-96)
Alternatively, if the victim, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:
*   begins to suffer from an illness for which there is no cure, or, enters a persistent vegetative state,  
*   suffers a complete loss of function to one of their senses or organs,  
*   loses the ability to speak or to reproduce, or  
*   a permanent change to their face,
texts.18:
the punishment determined above is increased to thrice its final amount (determined above).[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-97) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 5 years, or 8 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-98)
If the victim suffers a broken bone as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, the courts may increase the final punishment by up to half its original amount, depending on the vitality of the broken bone to daily life.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-99)
If the victim dies as a result of corporal punishment being used on them but the act does not meet the criteria for murder, the final punishment must be imprisonment for a term not less than 8 years and not more than 12 years. If the act was found to be "egregious", the term of imprisonment must be between 12 and 18 years.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-100)
In the United Kingdom, the law regarding domestic corporal punishment varies by jurisdiction.

Where in the world is smacking children illegal?
70 countries have taken the step of prohibiting all corporal punishment of children, including within the family home.
Sweden led the way in 1979. Since then, countries across the world have recognised that children deserve protection from physical punishment.
Yet in England, Northern Ireland, the USA, Canada and Australia, physical punishment by parents remains lawful in certain circumstances.
There is a difference between what is legally permitted and what we know about child development.
Children need boundaries, guidance and consequences. They do not need to experience physical pain to learn.
If we would not accept an adult being hit to teach them a lesson, why should we accept it for a child?
Protecting children from physical punishment is not about removing discipline. It is about recognising their right to safety, dignity and respect.

Until 2026, the Czech Republic had remained the only country in the European Union that does not outlaw child corporal punishment or plan to introduce such a law.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-37) On July 17, 2025, the president signed an amendment to the Civil Code, making corporal punishment of children explicitly prohibited by law, beginning January 1, 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-cz-16)
Corporal punishment in schools in Denmark became explicitly prohibited in 1967 and in 1985, parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children became outlawed through a new law which required parents "to protect their child from physical and psychological violence and other humiliating treatment".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-39) However, the law was believed to still support corporal punishment as there was a controversy whether the law permitted parents to punish their children physically or otherwise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-40) Therefore, after several years of debate, a new, clearer law came into force on 28 May 1997, providing that "_The child has right to care and security. It must be treated with respect for its person and must not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment_".
Denmark's autonomous territories, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, banned corporal punishment of children in 2007 and 2016, respectively.

School corporal punishment was banned in 1914.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-41) Parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was outlawed in 1969 when the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, stating that a "petty assault" was not punishable if committed by parents or others who exercise their right to chastise a child, was removed. In 1983, corporal punishment of children was explicitly banned.
In the Napoleonic era parents were explicitly allowed to physically punish their children. Spanking was previously popular, with 85% of French parents admitting to using it. However, in 2019, the National Assembly approved a bill introducing a complete ban on all forms of physical punishment of children and required mayors officiating at civil weddings to remind couples that violence against children is unlawful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-auto-7) The law makes corporal punishment a civil offense, not a criminal one.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-42)
School corporal punishment was prohibited in East Germany (which became part of the Federal Republic of Germany at the German reunification on 3 October 1990). In the Federal Republic (West Germany before reunification), it was prohibited at different times in its different states between 1975 and 1983.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-43)

In the Federal Republic of Germany, in 1980 it became prohibited for parents to educate their children with "degrading measures" (it was not clear exactly what "degrading" meant), of which the common interpretation was that corporal punishment of children was still permitted as long as it was not "degrading". On 1 July 1998, corporal punishment was outlawed through a new law stating that "Degrading educational measures, especially physical and psychological maltreatment, are inadmissible"; the common interpretation of that law was that parents still had some right to use corporal punishment on their children. In November 2000, that law was replaced with a new more clear and strict law stating that "_Children have right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological violence and other degrading educational measures are inadmissible._"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-45)
The 2006 enacted Law 3500/06 on the treatment of domestic violence prohibits the use of physical violence against a minor as a means of punishment in the context of his upbringing, with the explicit clarification - in the explanatory memorandum - that corporal punishment is not included. to the permissible penitentiary measures of article 1518 of the Civil Code and that its use entails for the parents the consequences of the bad exercise of parental care.
Specifically, Article 4 provides that physical violence against minors as a means of punishment in the context of their upbringing brings about the consequences of Article 1532 of the Civil Code. The explanatory memorandum to this article states, among other things: “The regulation of Article 4 makes it clear that corporal punishment against children is not included in the permissible punishment measures of Article 1518 of the Civil Code in accordance with modern pedagogical views. It constitutes a case of poor exercise of custody and for this reason brings about the application of article 1532 of the Civil Code. According to this article, in such a case, the court may order any appropriate measure. "Any act of inflicting pain or physical discomfort on a minor should be treated as physical violence, with the aim of punishing or controlling his behavior."

In Ireland, all forms of corporal punishment of children have been definitively outlawed since the passing of the Children First Act 2015.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46)Law in the Republic of Ireland inherited the pre-independence common law and statutes modelled on English law. These included allowance under common law of "physical chastisement" by teachers, and under the Children Act 1908 (8 Edw. 7. c. 67) of "reasonable chastisement" by parents and those _in loco parentis_.

In June 2021, the Spanish Parliament passed a new, pioneering child and adolescent protection law against all kinds of violence or abuse. It was championed by the British-Spanish pianist James Rhodes and the left-wing party Unidas Podemos, but eventually supported by all political groups in Parliament except Vox. A Code of Minors is also being drafted.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain3-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain4-83)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain0-80)
Sweden was the world's first nation to outlaw all corporal punishment of children in 1966, when the law that permitted parents to use corporal punishment of their children became removed and fully replaced with the constitution of assault under the Penal Code; however, even though the law no longer supported parents' right to use physical punishment of their children, it was believed to still be permitted (as there was no explicit ban). School corporal punishment was already banned since 1958.
On 1 July 1979, Sweden became the world's first nation to explicitly ban corporal punishment of children, through an amendment to the Parenthood and Guardianship Code which stated, "Children are entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. Children are to be treated with respect for their person and individuality and may not be subjected to corporal punishment or any other humiliating treatment." In Parliament - the law was supported 259 to 6 with 3 abstentions.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Modig-85) Corporal punishment in Sweden is not seen as a separate legal issue - but is handled according to the criteria for assault.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)

One thing that helped pave the way for the ban was a 1971 murder case where a 3-year-old girl was beaten to death by her stepfather. The case shook the general public and preventing child abuse became a political hot topic for years to come.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-87)
It is estimated that approximately 5% of Swedish children continue to be illegally spanked, however, in addition to being unlawful, physical punishment of children is now considered socially unacceptable.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-88)
On September 26, 2025, both chambers of the Federal Assembly approved the inclusion of "non-violent parenting" in Swiss law. The law forbids "physical punishment and other forms of degrading treatment". The Federal Council is to decide at the beginning of 2026 when the new law start to take effect.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-ch-17)
In Turkey, corporal punishment is unlawful, considered assault,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-89) and is punishable by imprisonment for a term not less than 1 year and not more than 3 years if none of the special cases below occur.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-90)
If the courts deem that any one of:

*   "the victim is physically or psychologically unable to defend themselves",  
*   the victim is the child of the perpetrator, or  
*   a weapon (which is defined to include "anything used in defense or offense"[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-91)) is used in the act is true, the punishment is increased by half of the original amount.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-92) If the courts deem that the perpetrator acted in a "fiendish" way, the punishment is increased to twice the original amount.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-93) If either one or both of these are true, it is said that the act was "egregious".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-94)
If the victim suffers, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:
*   persistent weakness in any of their senses or organs,  
*   persistent hardship in speaking,  
*   a permanent mark on their face, or  
*   a danger to their life,
the punishment determined above is increased to twice its final amount (determined above).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-95) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 3 years, or 5 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-96)
Alternatively, if the victim, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:
*   begins to suffer from an illness for which there is no cure, or, enters a persistent vegetative state,  
*   suffers a complete loss of function to one of their senses or organs,  
*   loses the ability to speak or to reproduce, or  
*   a permanent change to their face,

the punishment determined above is increased to thrice its final amount (determined above).[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-97) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 5 years, or 8 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-98)
If the victim suffers a broken bone as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, the courts may increase the final punishment by up to half its original amount, depending on the vitality of the broken bone to daily life.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-99)
If the victim dies as a result of corporal punishment being used on them but the act does not meet the criteria for murder, the final punishment must be imprisonment for a term not less than 8 years and not more than 12 years. If the act was found to be "egregious", the term of imprisonment must be between 12 and 18 years.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-100)
In the United Kingdom, the law regarding domestic corporal punishment varies by jurisdiction.

Where in the world is smacking children illegal?
70 countries have taken the step of prohibiting all corporal punishment of children, including within the family home.
Sweden led the way in 1979. Since then, countries across the world have recognised that children deserve protection from physical punishment.
Yet in England, Northern Ireland, the USA, Canada and Australia, physical punishment by parents remains lawful in certain circumstances.
There is a difference between what is legally permitted and what we know about child development.
Children need boundaries, guidance and consequences. They do not need to experience physical pain to learn.
If we would not accept an adult being hit to teach them a lesson, why should we accept it for a child?
Protecting children from physical punishment is not about removing discipline. It is about recognising their right to safety, dignity and respect.
